The basal metabolic rate of the Bushy-tailed hairy-footed gerbil (Gerbillurus vallinus) has been quantified through respirometry trials conducted at a stable ambient temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], yielding a resting oxygen consumption of 34.77 milliliters per hour [JOi = 34.77 milliliters per hour]. This value, which represents the maximum metabolic scope for this species, is broadly consistent with the energetic demands of small, arid-adapted murid rodents that must contend with substantial thermoregulatory costs in their native desert environments. Field-caught neonates of this species are remarkably altricial at parturition, with a recorded wet weight at birth of 4.5 grams [Wwb = 4.5 grams], a modest initial mass that necessitates an extended period of maternal investment and intensive lactation before the pups can achieve thermoregulatory independence. This small birth mass is typical of many Gerbillurus species and is closely linked to the constraints of producing offspring in unpredictable, resource-poor habitats.

Reproductive output in Gerbillurus vallinus appears to be structured around a high frequency of relatively small litters, a strategy well suited to the ephemeral productivity patterns of the Namib and Kalahari dunes it inhabits. Under controlled laboratory conditions designed to mimic the thermal regime of the species' active period, maintained at approximately 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], females produce litters ranging from 2 to 9 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 to 9 pups per litter]. Correspondingly, they are capable of generating an average of approximately 3.9 litters annually [F_R_i = approximately 3.9 litters annually], a reproductive tempo that is comparatively rapid for a rodent of this body size and that allows for rapid population recovery following periods of drought-induced quiescence. The maximum reproductive rate, integrating both litter size and frequency, is therefore substantial.

The ultimate body mass attained by adult females of this species, representing the maximum recorded adult weight in a well-nourished population, has been documented at 38.8 grams [Wwi = 38.8 grams]. This body size places Gerbillurus vallinus among the intermediate members of its genus, slightly larger than the sympatric Gerbillurus paeba but notably smaller than some other gerbilline rodents. The gestation period for this species, measured under stable environmental conditions at 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], extends for 21 days [tg = 21 days], a duration that is comparable to that reported for the congeneric Gerbillurus setzeri and which aligns with the general mammalian allometric relationship between maternal mass and gestation length. This relatively short gestation is consistent with the production of altricial young.

Following birth, the developmental trajectory of Gerbillurus vallinus proceeds through several distinct milestones. The time since birth at weaning has been recorded at 25 days [tx = 25 days] under captive conditions maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], a point at which the pups transition from exclusive reliance on milk to solid food and begin to achieve nutritional independence. This relatively brief suckling period is characteristic of small desert rodents, where rapid juvenile development confers a selective advantage in environments with short windows of resource abundance. The attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, follows a considerably longer interval: the time since birth at puberty is 152 days [tp = 152 days] when individuals are reared under the same thermal conditions of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This delay reflects the energetic investment required to complete somatic growth and accumulate sufficient body reserves before the onset of reproductive activity.

Longevity data for Gerbillurus vallinus, derived from captive colony records maintained under optimal conditions at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of 5.7 years [am = 5.7 years]. This value, equating to approximately 2080 days, is noteworthy for a rodent of its size, as many similarly massed murid species rarely exceed 2 to 3 years in captivity. The extended lifespan likely reflects a life-history strategy adapted to the predictability of the species' deep-sand dune habitats, where adult survival may be relatively high compared to surface-foraging small mammals in more exposed environments. Field studies in the southern Namib have reported maximum survival durations somewhat shorter than those achieved in captivity, but the potential for considerable longevity remains a defining feature of the species' demographic profile and underscores the slow pace of its life history relative to its reproductive rate.
